Sudargas Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Sudargas, Lithuania

Not demolished. Jews first settled in Sudargas in the mid-18th century; by 1856, the town's 627 Jewish residents made up 91% of the population. A nearby forest straddling the Lithuanian-Prussian border made smuggling a common livelihood, alongside timber rafting on the Nieman River and various shops. Economic decline after Lithuanian independence (1918-1940) drove most Jewish youth to emigrate or relocate to Kaunas, shrinking the town to just 257 residents by 1923. Religious life centered on a 19th-century wooden synagogue and Beit Midrash. Notably, architect Mosheh Yitshak Blokh (1893-1942), who designed an irrigation plan for the Negev desert, was born in Sudargas - Beer Sheva later named a street after him. Germany occupied the town on June 22, 1941; by early July, the roughly 30 remaining Jewish families' men were transferred to Šakiai and murdered alongside local men, followed by the women and children near Kiduliai village that August. The cemetery, established at the end of the 18th century atop one of Sudargas's mounds near the Nieman River, went out of use with the community's destruction; a 1944 farmhouse construction altered the hill's landscape. The site entered Lithuania's Cultural Property Register in 1998.
